steps.why: The classification runs on one test only — how many phases are present — so each definition is one sentence about the phase count.
common_mistakes: Writing 'same substance' instead of 'same phase'. The test is the phase, not the identity.
Confusing phase with physical state written per substance — all gases is ONE phase.
steps.memory_tip: Homo = same. All substances in the same phase.
steps.margin_note: The word phase must appear in the definition.

steps.label: Homogeneous — examples
lines: All the substances are gases — one phase.
steps.why: Both examples are all-gas equilibria, so every substance is in one phase; writing (g) under each substance is the evidence for that.
common_mistakes: Writing the equations without the (g) labels. The phase labels are what the example proves.
Using a one-way arrow. Both examples are equilibria, so the arrow is ⇌.
steps.memory_tip: HI and NH₃ — the two all-gas equilibria every textbook uses.
steps.margin_note: Phase label (g) under every substance earns this mark.

steps.label: Heterogeneous — definition
lines: of the reversible reaction are present in
steps.why: This is the complement of the first definition — the same phase test, failed: at least two phases are present at equilibrium.
common_mistakes: Claiming a heterogeneous equilibrium needs a liquid. Any two phases qualify — solid and gas is the common case.
steps.memory_tip: Hetero = different. More than one phase present.
steps.margin_note: One sentence — the mirror of the homogeneous definition.

steps.label: Heterogeneous — examples
lines: Solid and gas phases are present together.

lines.text: One phase = homogeneous; more than one phase = heterogeneous

steps.why: Both examples mix a solid with gases, so two phases are present in the same equilibrium — exactly what the definition requires; the boxed line closes the answer with the one-line test. One consequence is worth adding if the question asks for the expression: a pure solid or a pure liquid has a constant concentration, so it is LEFT OUT of the equilibrium constant. For CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g) the expressions are Kc = [CO₂] and Kp = pCO₂.
common_mistakes: Writing the phase labels wrong (CaCO₃ and CaO are solids, CO₂ is the gas).
Giving a second all-gas example here. A heterogeneous example must show two phases.
steps.memory_tip: Limestone in a kiln: solid in, solid plus gas out — the standard two-phase equilibrium.
steps.margin_note: Box the one-line test; it summarises both definitions.

insider_note: Definitions earn half, phase-labelled equations earn the rest — write (s) and (g) under every substance, because the labels are the evidence of the phase.
